title: Builder.io's /visual-edit skill turns local code into a Figma-like canvas
author: Steve (Builder.io)
essence: Steve (Builder.io) announces /visual-edit, an open-source skill that opens a running local app as URL-backed iframe screens on a Figma-style canvas so agents and humans can make visual edits. The self-thread then hands over the source (github.com/BuilderIO/skills), points to Agent-Native Design, gives the install command (npx @agent-native/core@latest skills add visual-edit) and answers how edits travel: the agent gets a prompt back containing a diff plus metadata such as each element's origin line of code. The captured replies are few but substantive and map straight onto that thread - Logan asks whether an edit 'lands as a diff or as a prompt back to the agent' (the thread answers: a prompt carrying a diff), while Abdul Wasey raises the real design-system risk: 'Dragging 1 card shouldn't quietly change all 20 screens.' One of the three captured replies is an unrelated ad. Sentiment: genuine curiosity with an unresolved component-scoping caveat. 27 replies, 799 likes, 1,082 bookmarks, 45.8K views.
summary: Reusable agent skills are becoming the distribution unit for dev tooling - a free OSS skill is how Builder.io puts its Design surface inside every coding agent.

title: Claude Code skill reverse-engineers any video into a remake recipe
author: Pratzyy
essence: Pratzyy's Claude Code skill /dissect takes any video apart and writes a recipe for remaking its format, demoed left-vs-right on a Kurzgesagt short. The self-thread expands the pitch: it breaks down picture (every cut, shot, caption style, transition), words (transcript, hook, story beats), voice (pace, pauses, pitch), sound (music, SFX, loudness) and audience (most-replayed moments, top comments), accepts YouTube/X/Instagram/TikTok links, and emits one blueprint .md anyone or any AI can follow; install is '/plugin marketplace add 0xpratzyy/dissect' and it is free/open source. The one substantive captured reply sets the quality bar - Thomas M.: 'I like the idea, but you have to say that we're not there yet. Kurzgesagt's one is way better. Intentional, concise... That 10%-5% is what elevates everything' - and Pratzyy concedes in-thread that it is currently a one-shot that improves with more detailed Opus prompts, adding 'this is the worst it will ever be'. A second reply is an unrelated conference ad. 26 replies, 231 likes, 322 bookmarks, 19.4K views.
summary: Reverse-engineering media into a reusable 'recipe' as an agent skill - a template for format-cloning and content-repurposing workflows.

title: Claude Code now supports mods: TypeScript plugins installed via /plugin
author: ClaudeDevs
essence: ClaudeDevs announces that Claude Code can now be modded - change how it behaves, customize the UI, swap in your own features - written in a few lines of TypeScript or generated by Claude, with mods shipping inside plugins and installed via /plugin in the CLI or desktop app. No replies were captured for this post (451 exist), so the substance comes from the six-tweet self-thread: Token Weather forecasts your context window with a sparkline of your last 12 turns; Blast Radius catches risky shell commands like rm -rf, git reset --hard or a force push before they run and shows what they would touch; Replay Theater records every file edit and lets you step through the diffs with /replay. The thread also warns that mods run with the same access to your machine as Claude Code, so only install trusted sources, links claude.ai/directory, offers pre-built sample mods in the Claude Code Playground repo, and notes the team already used mods to build /diff and AGENTS.md support. Biggest post in this slice: 451 replies, 1,375 reposts, 15,763 likes, 10,205 bookmarks, 2.4M views.
summary: Claude Code's plugin/mod layer is a platform moment: whoever ships the winning mods owns a distribution channel inside the agent itself.

title: ChatGPT can now build and deploy MCP servers on ChatGPT Sites
author: Tibo
essence: Tibo (OpenAI) quote-tweets Max Stoiber's launch to say you can now build and deploy MCP servers right through ChatGPT, then restrict their access to anyone you want or share them with the world; the quoted demo runs on '@sites create a todo list', which creates the MCP server, deploys it to Sites and turns it into a plugin. The quoted thread also carries Dishwasher's developer question about whether OpenAI-hosted infrastructure will eventually run backends for plugin extensions, since running a backend is the hard part. Captured replies turn skeptical: TEAGÁ 'nobody cares about Sites and Maps', Tucker King 'Hope people actually use the restrict button', and dearlordylord reporting a live approval bottleneck - his SRD 5e Oracle MCP 'is in approval loop for a month now' (a fourth captured reply is a spam ad). So the debate is about gating and distribution, not the tech. 414 replies, 4,990 likes, 2,156 bookmarks, 768.8K views.
summary: MCP servers become one-click hosted products inside ChatGPT - distribution for MCP builders just got much bigger; watch the hosting, permissions and backend story.

title: OpenClaw cut 400k LOC of tests with a test-audit skill, coverage intact
author: Peter Steinberger 🦞
essence: Peter Steinberger reports that OpenClaw deleted around 400k LOC of its own tests with almost no change in code coverage, crediting a test-audit skill (linked card: openclaw/.agents/skills/test-audit/SKILL.md). His diagnosis: modern models love writing tests for every tiny change even when those tests aren't useful. The self-thread adds the actual technique - 'If you just tell the agent to clean up, it will stop far too early. Give it an ambitious goal', e.g. 'remove 20% of the least useful tests while maintaining code coverage within 2%' - and five days later he notes 'That /goal is still running.' David Cramer's reply extends the argument: models 'also love rewriting tests when they change code as if the reason for those tests in the first place wasnt to prevent regressions'. Sentiment is broad agreement about AI test bloat. 230 replies, 6,699 likes, 10,791 bookmarks, 1.3M views.
summary: Sharpest AI-quality insight in the set: agent-written tests inflate coverage without value, and an audit skill is a cheap way to claw the bloat back.

title: Movie archive spreadsheet: 1300+ films, 800 Blu-ray remuxes, links never expire
author: vilibazmio
essence: vilibazmio's updated public spreadsheet (card: docs.google.com / vilibazmio_archive.xlsx) claims 1,300+ archived movies, nearly 800 Blu-ray remuxes and links that 'will never expire'. The self-thread pre-empts two criticisms: uploads have been live over a year and 'films that aren't mainstream almost never get copyrighted', plus a clarification that the archive 'isn't meant to be used as a streaming platform' - download before watching, and the preview video it sometimes generates is lower quality. Replies split between gratitude and legal unease: snvy asks 'what is the copyright status of these movies?' and warns that enough copyright-holder demands could force archive.org to lock the uploader's account, while Sarvar reports a broken entry ('The Pear Tree (1998) by Dariush Mehrjui... is just an image of the film'). Engagement dwarfs the debate: 114,149 likes, 155,945 bookmarks, 10,079 reposts, 2.8M views, 166 replies.
summary: One evergreen spreadsheet outperformed almost everything in this set - durable, save-worthy link assets work; note the obvious copyright risk before emulating it.

title: One prompt, 8 hours: Claude Code generated an entire app launch video
author: Leon Lin
essence: Leon Lin gave Claude Code (Opus 5.5) one prompt to make a launch video for a fake calendar app and claims everything you see and hear - name, logo, UI, animations, soundtrack, sound effects - is code, after it 'cooked for about 8h'. The self-thread drops the repo (github.com/Leonxlnx/claude-launchvideo) with code, soundtrack and video in it, clarifies the 8h includes reviews and recording (the cloud agent took 30 min), and the author concedes the criticism himself: 'the soundeffects and bg soundtrack don't really match this type of video'. Replies agree on visuals but not audio: mehdi calls it 'by far the best launch video generated by opus 5.5 by a mile', Witti says it is 'master-class' yet dislikes the AI-made music in these videos, and Arthur jokes 'at this point i don't even know if people are joking or not'. 86 replies, 1,279 likes, 1,315 bookmarks, 90.1K views.
summary: End-to-end launch-video production from one prompt is now a working demo - worth planning agent-generated video into your own launch pipeline.

title: MoneyPrinterTurbo: free AI tool that turns a topic into short videos
author: Innopro
essence: Innopro hypes MoneyPrinterTurbo, a free tool from a Chinese developer that (claimed) passed 100,000 GitHub stars and turns a topic into finished TikToks, Reels and Shorts: give it a topic, AI writes the script, generates voice and subtitles, finds visuals and assembles the video. It quote-tweets Mike's roundup of all free AI resources in 2026, which is what frames this as a free-AI win. There is no self-thread, so the four captured replies carry the reaction and they are thin: notgwapo worries about misuse - 'wonder how long till everyone's using it to spam stuff' - Tom asks 'What is the name of this tool?' (no captured reply answers it), and one reply is an unrelated hotel ad. Sentiment is hype plus spam anxiety rather than technical scrutiny. 10 replies, 481 likes, 813 bookmarks, 65.4K views.
summary: MoneyPrinterTurbo is the current default for automated short-form video - useful as the baseline competitor if you build anywhere near AI video.

title: Claude recreated a SpaceX explainer video in another video's style
author: Julian Alvarez
essence: Julian Alvarez downloaded DreW's animated video (quoted credit: 'Made with @claudeai Opus 5.5'), handed it to Claude with 'create an animated video in the style of the attached video. make a video that visualizes how a SpaceX rocket works', left it overnight and woke up to the result. The self-thread shows he already sees the business angle - 'unreal, huge content opportunities unlocked here' and 'so curious to try this as an editing style for reels' - and answers a cost question with the runtime: 'not sure but it took 1hr and 12 min'. Replies are uniformly amazed with a practical undertow: 'wtf this is great', 'the jump from prompt to something you'd actually watch is wild', 'instant rocket explainer, straight up magic', alongside Viz asking 'How much was $$'. 9 replies, 437 likes, 381 bookmarks, 45.4K views.
summary: Style-transfer video generation from a single reference clip is a repeatable pattern for explainer content - one overnight agent run, no editor.

title: Theo's guide to getting the most out of Opus 5.5
author: Theo - t3.gg
essence: Theo (t3.gg) drops his guide to maximizing success with Opus 5.5, crediting Addy Osmani's writeup. The self-thread supplies what the main tweet lacks: a link tweet to the writeup (card: 'Getting the most out of Opus 5.5 in Claude and Claude Code' on the claude.dev blog) and his blunt rule of thumb - 'If you're struggling to identify when to use each model, just use Opus 5.5. The cases where the others make sense are incredibly rare.' Replies are mostly celebratory and slightly needy: Addy Osmani 'Great video and more to come!', Bilal Bakr 'Just what I was waiting for! Now we need a vs Fable & Astra vid', and Ansh Nanda asking 'What's the link to the write up?' - a gap the thread's link tweet fills. 46 replies, 1,478 likes, 1,246 bookmarks, 130.2K views.
summary: A distilled Opus 5.5 usage guide from Theo is worth an hour before your next build - treat it as the practical companion to the model's release notes.

title: $3.6 and 16 minutes: Opus 5.5 rendered a philosophy animation
author: Harveen Singh Chadha
essence: Harveen Singh Chadha reveals the 'embarrassingly simple' prompt behind his Opus 5.5 clip - 'Create a pure javascript animation. 30s-60s whimsical hand drawn collage style with appropriate audio on the topic what is the purpose of life?' - and states the economics: one shot, Opus wrote the script and everything, 16 minutes, 19k tokens, $3.6, quoting his earlier post of the finished animation. There is no self-thread, but the replies are the most pointed in this set: Kamaljot Singh challenges the numbers directly ('19K tokens and $3.6 cost? Math ain't mathing'), AT asks 'What was the effort level?', Levi asks 'What JS library does it use?', chriscardoza asks 'are you able to share the git repo?', and Neatprompts questions how much Opus authored. Gojoooo pushes back positively on the low cost. Net sentiment: impressed but asking for receipts nobody posted. 13 replies, 517 likes, 691 bookmarks, 50.9K views.
summary: A concrete cost benchmark for AI-generated animation - ~19K tokens and $3.6 for a 30-60s piece is handy for content budgeting.

title: Tool scrapes any product URL into a markdown repo of features and pricing
author: Mikhaeel
essence: Mikhaeel built a tool powered by Jev that takes a product URL and extracts its features, business logic, ICP, messaging and pricing strategy into a markdown file you can copy straight into a repo - fast competitive teardown for founders rather than engineering. The self-thread adds the try-link (card: 'Vicaura - Product logic to markdown') and the pitch 'You can just copy paste products now lol'. Replies validate demand and echo the reverse-engineering framing: Vyom 'damn I have to try this !!!', Aman 'bro just made reverse engineering way easier', and Sankalp Sinha saying he featured the post on the Jev.Store community directory. So the conversation is adoption-positive, with no accuracy objections raised. 48 replies, 280 likes, 536 bookmarks, 100.7K views.
summary: Instant competitor teardown from a URL is a handy pre-PRD step - useful for positioning work before you write a single line of spec.

title: Aikido open-sources Altar-1, an open-weight security model for on-prem use
author: Aikido
essence: Aikido announces Altar-1, its first open-weight security model, pitched as 'frontier-grade defensive AI, built to deploy. Own your own security'. The self-thread does the heavy lifting: it links the full announcement ('Aikido Altar: open-weight AI for sovereign security'), a deployable Hugging Face repo (AikidoSec/altar-1), and a naming aside about Ghent's 1432 Adoration of the Mystic Lamb altarpiece. The captured reply tab is thin - one genuine 'nice' from SIGKITTEN plus an unrelated job-board ad among the 86 replies - so this is a reach post whose engagement (515.3K views, 257 reposts, 1,540 likes, 1,168 bookmarks) comes from the launch itself rather than from debate. Worth following for the open-weight, deploy-on-prem security angle.
summary: Open-weight, deploy-on-prem security AI shows enterprises increasingly want models inside their own perimeter - relevant if you ship security or compliance features.

title: Medium: the full Claude Code setup for bug bounty hunting, prompts included
author: Coffin
essence: Coffin (lostsec) shares his longest Medium article yet, consolidating the methods, setups and workflows from his three recent Claude videos with every prompt included so readers can copy, paste and try them, specifically for bug bounty hunting. The self-thread answers a setup question in four words: 'claude with openrouter'. The captured replies show what practitioners actually want to know: APC_MOD asks whether 'abliterated open weights + OpenCode would be a good setup for BB' - i.e. uncensored local models plus an open agent - and xofin reports a practical blocker, Burp Suite activation failing under WSL 2. Sentiment is engaged and tool-shopping rather than skeptical. 19 replies, 678 likes, 658 bookmarks, 29.1K views.
summary: A consolidated, prompt-included Claude Code workflow - reasonable reference material if you are formalizing an agent setup for security work.

title: Spotify launches Xirp, a vendor-neutral agentic dev environment
author: Spotify Engineering
essence: Spotify Engineering launches Xirp, a vendor-neutral agentic development environment that manages agent sessions across Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Codex in one place, already used by 1,300+ Spotify engineers and now available for anyone to try; the self-thread links Tyson Singer's piece ('Spotify Portal - One source of truth for engineers & agents'). The captured replies are mostly incredulity rather than adoption: 'Spotify? The AI Company?', 'would it sing to me while i code?', 'Spotify building an IDE wasn't in my bingo card', 'Why is Spotify trying to hop on the AI bandwagon', kitze's 'Bro stay in your lane and fix your... music app', and 'what the fuck lol'. A few are substantive - Jason Kneen asks 'Closed source? Seriously?' (nothing in the launch claims open source), Marcelo Lima wants a way to code his own Spotify UI, Teknium wants to see Hermes on it, Logan Juhl jokes about everyone's 'Xirp Wrapped'. Still the biggest reach in this set: 636 replies, 2,063 reposts, 11,566 likes, 9,457 bookmarks, 5.3M views.
summary: Vendor-neutral session management across Claude, Gemini and Codex is the layer large orgs are standardizing on - Spotify open-sourcing it is a strong signal for multi-agent tooling.

title: brandpull: npx CLI that pulls any site's branding kit in 10 seconds
author: Suraj Gaud
essence: Suraj Gaud introduces brandpull, an npx CLI that pulls any website's branding kit in about 10 seconds for agents and humans ('npx brandpull'). The self-thread adds the GitHub repo (suraj-xd/brandpull) and a second project link (Shoogle, a shadcn UI components and blocks search engine). Replies are positive and competitive rather than critical: Lokendra says he was 'thinking of something similar but on ui where user can search brand of any site and it lists all of its components like cards, tabs, dialog etc', Bharath shares his own attempt (typescrape.vercel.app), dhru plans to use it 'fossure' to fix a landing page, and the rest are short praise ('okay thats VALUE', a goat emoji). 8 replies, 112 likes, 190 bookmarks, 27.3K views.
summary: A tiny CLI returning structured branding JSON - handy whenever an agent-built page needs a real site's colors, fonts and logos without a signup.

title: Three tech-drama shows: The Playlist, The Billion Dollar Code, Super Pumped
author: Olaoluwa (DhP.)
essence: No replies to this tweet itself - it sits as a reply inside a conversation about finishing HBO's Silicon Valley: @archiexzzz 'just finished watching silicon valley and im liberated. best series evaahh...' and @shravann44 'I fear completing it, started 2 years ago. Scared of not finding anything similar to it.' The bookmarked tweet is the answer to that fear - a bare list of three substitutes: The Playlist (Netflix's Spotify story), The Billion Dollar Code (Google versus Urijah) and Super Pumped: The Battle For Uber - with no commentary, links or media. It functions as a personal watchlist rather than a shared recommendation: 0 replies of its own, 2 likes, 5 bookmarks, 173 views.
summary: Mundane watchlist; only worth noting as startup-origin drama references for storytelling.

title: 'Judge me' idea: GPT-4 analyses your tweets to judge your character
author: Surendhar
essence: No replies and no thread of its own: this tweet is an idea pitched into @krishnerkar's challenge - 'i'm bored, drop some random crazy ideas/experiments to build with GPT-4. i'll pick the one with most likes and ship it in 24 hours'. The proposal is concrete enough to ship in a day: the user enters a Twitter user id, the app fetches that account's posted tweets and liked tweets (images included, since GPT-4 had just gained image support), then judges the person's character from them - 'Name it judge me!'. It drew no visible traction in this capture: 0 replies, 3 likes, 1 bookmark, 502 views, which is what you'd expect from a one-off reply in a busy build-in-24h thread.
summary: Mundane early GPT-4 gimmick idea; little value beyond an example of personality-analysis demos.

title: Meme: 'Have you tried this in any of your projects?' - source LinkedIn
author: Akash Jha | 🇮🇳
essence: Akash Jha posts a video meme copied from LinkedIn - 'Have you tried this in any of your projects? 😂😂 source: Linkedin' - joking about snippets and advice that circulate between LinkedIn and dev teams, and adds only 'yeah😂😂' to his own thread. The captured replies show the joke landing as ironic adoption rather than critique: Aryan Srivastava 'That's seems fun to do will try for sure', Haider 'I saw this post yesterday on LinkedIn. I'm definitely going to use this in my next project. Hilarious', Sachin and amish both promising it for their next project, Manish suggesting 'Awesome for validation use', and a Hinglish punchline - 'Agr user mood pe na ho toh, System tod dalega!' Sentiment: playful and self-aware. 74 replies, 1,268 likes, 136 reposts, 163 bookmarks.
summary: Mundane meme; only useful as a reminder of how LinkedIn content propagates into engineering culture.

title: ego (lite) lets GPT learn skills by watching YouTube tutorials
author: ego
essence: ego announces that GPT can now learn skills by watching YouTube tutorials with ego (lite): GPT-5.6 Sol watched a tutorial at 1.5x, switched Spaces and recreated the quiz workflow in Google Forms from memory in 36m50s using 64 ego-browser calls, claimed 'totally executable'. There is no self-thread, so the three captured replies carry the reception and they are uniformly positive: a Chinese-language viewer '我擦 还能这样玩 可以多来点这样的showcase哈哈' (whoa, didn't know you could do this - want more showcases), RAZA 'This is a fascinating step toward AI learning workflows by observation', and Alice 'learning a skill from a YouTube tutorial and recreating it end to end is seriously impressive'. No skepticism captured, but reach is small: 5 replies, 33 likes, 27 bookmarks, 4,402 views.
summary: Agents acquiring skills from YouTube is a real distribution channel for tutorials - worth testing if your product needs browser automation learned from video.

title: Shaders goes open source: 200+ WebGPU components, export code for any framework
author: shaders
essence: shaders (@npm_i_shaders) open-sources 200+ WebGPU components — use in client sites, templates, products or libraries and export code for any framework, free (github.com/shader-effects-inc/shaders; announcement at shaders.com/updates/shaders-is-open-source). Self-thread adds the agent angle: coding agents write raw WGSL that underperforms in production, so building on production-tested components means better shaders, faster workflow and real performance. Replies show immediate adoption: Bin Liu is adding them to HyperFrames Studio today, Josh Millgate is adding shader backgrounds to ultramock, and TypeGPU's Iwo Plaza calls it a huge move; Audiencon notes open source plus exportable code removes framework lock-in. Post drew 66 replies, 251 reposts, ~3K likes, 3.8K bookmarks and 186K views with a video demo.
summary: Save the repo and announcement; the agents-building-on-tested-components framing is the reusable pattern for shipping WebGPU without hand-tuning WGSL.

title: Never use staccato sentences in landing pages — design prompt of the day
author: Michael
essence: Michael (@michael_chomsky) design prompt of the day: LLMs write staccato sentences ('More reliable. Less expensive.' / 'Sleep better. Live longer.') — tell your agent to never use staccato sentences in landing pages (OP misspells it 'stacatto' and admits he checked the spelling and still got it wrong; correct spelling is staccato). Replies carry the real value: Seth traces it to a decade of DTC landing pages, Apple wrote 'thinner. lighter. faster.' before LLMs; David Qu adds 'it's not X, it's Y' to the ban list; John says every landing page reads like a pharma ad now; Asmir warns banning one tic just swaps in the next, so paste a paragraph you like to copy instead; Mika shares a Design.md winner, 'refrain from point & shoot terminology' (stop robotically explaining why the feature exists); Vincent asks why no good human-writer skill exists. 24 replies, 16 reposts, 753 likes, 677 bookmarks.
summary: Copy-paste prompt rule for landing pages, plus two steals: also ban 'it's not X, it's Y' and give the agent a liked-paragraph example instead of pure bans.

title: Leviathan: open-source indexer lets agents search 1M records in ~436 tokens
author: joshua
essence: joshua (@joshuagunnn) open-sources Leviathan (github.com/elstongun/leviathan): one Rust binary so agents search any-size databases without reading them — point at JSONL, CSV or SQLite, or pipe Postgres, MySQL, DuckDB or Mongo; it infers the schema, builds a full-text index and returns short cited cards at ~450 tokens whether 10K or 1M rows. Self-thread: agents reason over five records but drown in a million (grep, paging APIs, dumping whole history into context); at 1M rows 99% of questions get a relevant record in the top 5 with 33ms median, worst case 602 tokens versus grep's 9.7M; under ~100K rows grep is honestly fine. CLI first, MCP optional, because MCP schemas tax every session while a skill file costs zero tokens until called; works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor. Replies: skeptic snow flags it as just FTS5/BM25, nothing new (fair prior-art caution); mbrochh asks for folder and docs indexing beyond DBs; badguyty asks about NoSQL and log streams; OP floats a $10/month hosted auto-index version. 72 replies, 179 reposts, 2.5K likes, 3.7K bookmarks.
summary: Save for agent-plus-large-data work; the token math (436 vs 107K) and CLI-first-over-MCP rule are the keepers — verify BM25/FTS limits before adopting.

title: Devin Dreaming plus Agent Memory Repo: Git-versioned memory graph as OSS standard
author: Cognition
essence: Cognition (@cognition) introduces Dreaming: across sessions Devin builds a memory graph of how you work, and at night it self-improves that memory to remove stale records and discover latent information; alongside it they are creating an OSS standard, Agent Memory Repo (cognition.com/agent-memory-repo; explainer at devin.ai/blog/memory-and-dreaming). Self-thread: memory records live in files versioned with Git — a simple primitive that unlocks a message board across agent sessions — and in early tests a swarm of Devins used the memory to coordinate at large scale without being prompted. Replies: Jared Zoneraich and Chris Wozniczek say they can retire their git-brain and studio-brain repos, with Chris running parallel Devins on interconnected Linear tasks and calling the coordination a massive unlock; Corey Ward hopes it fixes PR reviews flagging non-issues; band.eth asks whether it hallucinates context from old logs (open risk); Elara calls the OSS standard a huge move. 126 replies, 331 reposts, 2.3K likes, 2.2K bookmarks with a video.
summary: Watch the OSS Agent Memory Repo spec — Git-versioned memory files as a cross-session message board is the pattern to copy even outside Devin.

title: Gyotaku: ctrl+f for your screenshots folder, fully offline and open source
author: xevrion
essence: xevrion (@xevrion_the1) built ctrl+f for the screenshots folder: type any word that appeared in an image and it surfaces in milliseconds, fully offline and open source (github.com/xevrion/gyotaku; now on Windows via a one-line PowerShell install, screenshots never leave the machine). Replies surface the important alternatives: ayushbuilds shipped the same idea months ago as neurasnip (github.com/Ayushkumar111/neurasnip) with semantic search by text or image; Harsh Navani shipped a Mac version yesterday at dejashot.com; Abhishek Kothari notes offline matters because half those screenshots hold private content; Muhammad Kashan Ashraf notes he could have charged but open-sourced it. 152 replies, 72 reposts, 1.3K likes, 809 bookmarks with a demo video.
summary: Grab gyotaku for Windows and offline OCR search; compare neurasnip (semantic) and dejashot (Mac) before committing — offline privacy is the deciding feature.

title: ASD-STE100 skill kills terminal slop: agents write in Simplified Technical English
author: pili 🪴
essence: pili (@0xpili_) quotes Karpathy's Oct 2 thread on understanding LLM outputs (tip: ask the LLM to explain in ASD-STE100) and ships the skill: agents write in ASD-STE100, Simplified Technical English, and terminal slop drops drastically (github.com/0xpili/simplified-technical-english). Self-thread: the skill is much better short-term, unsure long-term; invites try-and-report feedback. Replies: Steven Elliott calls it life-changing; Piyush tried it and asks whether the skill beats just asking the agent for ASD-STE output; Alpha Desk asks why not a one-liner in agents.md; Farzin wants a copywriting skill (GPT is bad at copy); interplato asks about token limits; danigonlinea considered output-styles instead; Neil Hartner counters with placebo-effect skepticism. 59 replies, 150 reposts, 3.3K likes, 6.1K bookmarks, 320K views.
summary: Try the skill for agent-written prose; the open question — skill vs one-liner vs output style — is worth testing yourself.

title: Interview take-home for an Indian frontier AI lab: inference on hardware (inference-forge)
author: Shashvat Singh
essence: Shashvat Singh built a take-home project for an Indian frontier AI lab interview: inference on hardware, a genuinely cool problem statement (repo: inference-forge, an adaptive batch inference pipeline). Self-thread: the lab had a lax AI-use policy but you had to understand what the code meant; praises interviews that skip DSA norms and put you in real problem-solver shoes. Replies: Almichael asks if it was take-home and what the AI policy was; Saurabh says frontier-lab problems are most fun near real systems; Tej jokes every AI-scaffolded project is named 'forge'. 5 replies, 75 likes, 140 bookmarks.
summary: A concrete inference-on-hardware interview project template; check the repo for batching patterns.

title: REA: open-source toolkit gives your AI agent reverse-engineering via MCP and CLI
author: Vaishnavi
essence: Vaishnavi (@_vmlops) launches REA (Reverse Engineer Anything): an open-source toolkit bringing reverse-engineering to AI agents via MCP and CLI — decompile apps and native binaries, trace execution and inspect evidence, recreate features for your own stack (github.com/morluto/rea). Replies are thin (thanks plus ads), so the value is the launch itself. 80 replies, 657 reposts, 6.2K likes, 9.1K bookmarks, 300K views.
summary: Save for agent-driven RE work; verify MCP tool quality before wiring it into your agent.

title: Every vibe coder's SEO prompt is actually the whole checklist — paste into Claude Code
author: Suraj Sharma
essence: Suraj Sharma's joke SEO prompt for vibe coders ('Rank #1 by Friday. Make no mistakes.' after SSR, sitemap, Search Console, robots, noindex, redirects, 404s, canonicals, meta descriptions, one H1, FAQ schema, breadcrumbs, orphans, alt text, WebP, CLS, sub-2s loads, de-slop, author bio, backlinks) is actually the whole checklist — bookmark it, paste into Claude Code, and do the last two (bio, backlinks) yourself. Self-thread: live-page checks should be mandatory; vibe sites optimize for browsers over search engines; technical SEO gets you discovered, trust gets you chosen. Replies: Shawn adds where real wins start (canonicals, JSON-LD, og:image); Jamie says SSR is the biggest fix since client-rendered pages look blank to Google; catman frames it as doors-and-signs vs trust; Ganesh reports only 3 pages indexed after 7 months. 62 replies, 172 reposts, 3.2K likes, 9.2K bookmarks.

title: Deleted 800K lines of unit tests from the monorepo: 3 hypotheses on why tests hurt agents
author: Sherwood
essence: Sherwood (@shcallaway) deleted 800K lines of unit tests from the sazabi monorepo with three hypotheses: tests lock in slop by making code hard to change, slow dev cycles via extra agent work and CI time, and waste money via agent tokens and useless CI runs — results to follow.
